## Bismarck's Alliance System and the Isolation of France
Germany united in 1871. That changed Europe's power balance.
Bismarck wanted to keep France alone. France had lost Alsace-Lorraine and felt bitter.
In 1879, Germany made the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary. Italy joined in 1882, making the Triple Alliance.
The Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 kept Russia neutral. That meant Russia would not fight Germany.
When Kaiser Wilhelm II fired Bismarck in 1890, he let the Reinsurance Treaty end. France then made an alliance with Russia in 1894. That put Germany in danger of a two-front war.
Britain stopped being alone. The Entente Cordiale in 1904 settled colonial fights with France. The Anglo-Russian Entente in 1907 settled rivalries in Persia, Afghanistan, and Tibet.
These agreements had no military duty. But by 1907, Europe had two armed camps: the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente.
An arms race grew. Germany built up its navy, and Britain launched HMS Dreadnought in 1906. The Schlieffen Plan planned a fast attack on France through Belgium.
Crises made trust worse. The First Moroccan Crisis in 1905-06 ended badly for Germany. Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia in 1908, and the Agadir Crisis in 1911 nearly caused war.
Bismarck's system kept peace while he was in charge. After he left, it fell apart.
Key: Bismarck built alliances to isolate France.
Key: Dual Alliance (1879) with Austria-Hungary, then Italy joined in 1882 to form the Triple Alliance.
Key: Reinsurance Treaty (1887) kept Russia neutral.
Key: After Bismarck was dismissed in 1890, the Reinsurance Treaty lapsed, and France allied with Russia in 1894.
Key: Britain ended its isolation with the Entente Cordiale (1904) and the Anglo-Russian Entente (1907).
Key: By 1907, Europe had two armed camps: Triple Alliance and Triple Entente.

## The Triple Entente and the Two Armed Camps
Germany united in 1871 and changed Europe's power balance. Bismarck, the German Chancellor, wanted to keep France weak because France lost Alsace-Lorraine and felt bitter.
Bismarck made alliances to isolate France. In 1879 Germany and Austria-Hungary made the Dual Alliance. Italy joined in 1882, forming the Triple Alliance. The Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 kept Russia neutral.
In 1890 Kaiser Wilhelm II fired Bismarck and let the Reinsurance Treaty end. France saw its chance and made the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894. This meant Germany could face war on two fronts.
Britain gave up its 'splendid isolation'. The Entente Cordiale of 1904 settled colonial disputes with France over Egypt and Morocco. The Anglo-Russian Entente of 1907 settled rivalries in Persia, Afghanistan, and Tibet.
These agreements had no formal military duties, but by 1907 Europe was split into two armed camps: the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente. Local quarrels became matters of continental prestige.
An arms race grew. German naval laws of 1898 and 1900, led by Admiral Tirpitz, challenged British sea power. The launch of HMS Dreadnought in 1906 made battleship rivalry worse.
On land, the Schlieffen Plan of 1905, refined by Moltke the Younger, planned a quick attack on France through Belgium. Military spending rose after 1900, and general staffs gained influence.
Crises broke trust. In the First Moroccan Crisis (1905-06), Wilhelm II landed at Tangier to challenge France. The Algeciras Conference of 1906 humiliated Germany.
In 1908 Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina, angering Serbia and forcing Russia to back down. The Agadir Crisis of 1911, when the German gunboat Panther appeared off Morocco, nearly caused war.
Takeaway: By 1907, two armed camps faced off, and each crisis made war more likely.

Key: Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck and let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse, leading to the Franco-Russian Alliance (1894).
Key: Britain's ententes with France (1904) and Russia (1907) formed the Triple Entente.
Key: Arms race: German naval laws, Dreadnought, Schlieffen Plan.
Key: Crises: First Moroccan, Bosnia, Agadir.

## The Balkan Wars and the Assassination in Sarajevo
The Balkan Wars of 1912-13 pushed the Ottoman Empire out of Europe. Serbia came out bigger and stronger, and Austria-Hungary saw that as a danger.
On 28 June 1914, Gavrilo Princip shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo. Princip was a Bosnian Serb tied to the Black Hand group.
Austria-Hungary used the killing as its excuse to act. Its foreign minister, Count Berchtold, got Germany's 'blank cheque' on 5-6 July — a promise of full support against Serbia.
The July Crisis moved fast. Austria-Hungary sent Serbia an ultimatum on 23 July, made so harsh it would be refused. Serbia's calm reply on 25 July was turned down, and both sides began to mobilise.
Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July. Russia's Tsar Nicholas II ordered full mobilisation on 30 July, even after trading telegrams with Germany's Kaiser Wilhelm II.
Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August. The Schlieffen Plan forced Germany to invade Belgium, whose neutrality Britain had promised to protect since 1839.
Britain's foreign minister, Sir Edward Grey, sent final warnings, but they were ignored. Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914.
Who is to blame? In 1961, Fritz Fischer argued that German leaders wanted to dominate Europe. That reopened the debate after the Treaty of Versailles had blamed Germany in Article 231.
Most historians now say the war came from a mix: alliances, militarism, imperial rivalry, and Balkan nationalism. The choices of leaders in summer 1914 turned one murder into a world war.

## The July Crisis and the Outbreak of War
The Balkan Wars pushed the Ottoman Empire out of Europe. Serbia grew bigger and stronger, and Austria-Hungary saw that as a danger.
On 28 June 1914, Gavrilo Princip killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife in Sarajevo. Austria used this as a reason to act.
Austria asked Germany for support. Germany gave a 'blank cheque' on 5-6 July, promising help no matter what.
Austria sent Serbia an ultimatum on 23 July, made to be refused. Serbia's calm reply on 25 July was rejected, and both sides began to mobilize.
Austria declared war on Serbia on 28 July. Russia then ordered full mobilization on 30 July, even after the tsar and the Kaiser traded telegrams.
Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August. The Schlieffen Plan forced Germany to invade Belgium.
Britain had promised to protect Belgium since 1839. Germany's invasion broke that promise, so Britain declared war on 4 August 1914.
Historians still argue about who caused the war. Fritz Fischer said Germany wanted to rule Europe. Others point to alliances, militarism, and nationalism.
